title: Quiz: DMAIC Framework and Root Cause Analysis Tools

questions.text: In a Pareto chart of defect types, the cumulative percentage line crosses 80% after the third category. This means:
options: The top three defect types account for 80% of all defects — focus on these to achieve the greatest improvement
You must fix all defect types, because fixing only 80% of defects still leaves 20% unresolved
The data collection was incomplete — a good process should have all causes below 80%
The bottom three categories are more important because they are undercounted
questions.explanation: The Pareto principle (80/20 rule) identifies the 'vital few' causes that produce most of the effect. Crossing 80% after three categories means those three types generate 80% of defects. Eliminating them yields disproportionate improvement. Trying to fix all types simultaneously dilutes effort and slows improvement.

questions.text: During a 5 Whys analysis, a team reaches the answer 'The operator did not follow the procedure.' The facilitator asks Why again. What type of root cause is the team most likely approaching?
options: A human error root cause — individual accountability is the appropriate corrective action
A systemic or process-design failure — such as an unclear SOP, inadequate training, or a missing error-proofing mechanism
A measurement system failure — the operator's errors indicate gauge drift
An environmental factor — ambient conditions affected the operator's performance
questions.explanation: In 5 Whys analysis, 'operator error' is almost never a true root cause — it is a symptom of a system failure. Asking Why one more level typically reveals: unclear procedure, lack of training, poor workstation design, or absence of mistake-proofing. Blaming individuals without fixing the system guarantees recurrence.

questions.text: A Six Sigma team is about to analyse 6 months of process data to identify root causes. They then discover their measurement system has %GRR = 45%. At which DMAIC phase is this discovery most damaging, and why?
options: Define — because the project charter will need to be rewritten
Analyse — because the data used for root cause analysis is unreliable; findings may be artefacts of measurement noise
Improve — because DOE results will be invalid if discovered here
Control — because control chart signals cannot be trusted
questions.explanation: Discovering %GRR = 45% during Analyse means all the process data collected in Measure is untrustworthy — the measurement error (45% of tolerance) is so large it could mask or create apparent patterns. The correct place to validate the measurement system is in Measure (before data collection), using a Gauge R&R study. Discovering it in Analyse typically forces a costly restart of the Measure phase.

questions.text: Which DMAIC phase is primarily responsible for ensuring that improvements are permanent after the project closes?
options: Define — because a strong project charter prevents regression
Analyse — because understanding root causes ensures they cannot return
Improve — because the pilot study proves the solution works
Control — through control charts, updated SOPs, mistake-proofing, and handover to the process owner
questions.explanation: Control is the sustainability phase. It uses statistical process control (control charts) for ongoing monitoring, updated Standard Operating Procedures to encode the new method, mistake-proofing (Poka-yoke) to make errors impossible, and formal handover to ensure the process owner, not the project team, sustains the gain after the project ends.

questions.text: In a fishbone (Ishikawa) diagram, the causes closest to the fish head (main spine junction) are always the most important root causes and should be prioritised first.
questions.explanation: A fishbone diagram is a brainstorming and organisation tool — it does not rank causes by importance or probability. All bones and sub-causes are hypotheses that require data collection and analysis (e.g., Pareto chart, hypothesis tests) to prioritise. Proximity to the spine in the diagram has no statistical meaning.
